title: Backup Security and Data Sovereignty in an AI-Driven World | AvePoint
summary: Learn how air gaps, immutable storage, and data sovereignty strengthen backup security for Microsoft 365 and multicloud data in an AI-driven world.
body_markdown:
## **Key Takeaways**


- **Air gaps and immutability solve different problems.** Isolation limits the path from a compromised production environment, while immutability blocks alteration during the configured retention period.


- **Logical air gaps fit cloud and SaaS environments.** Separate backup identities, permissions, and storage reduce dependence tape handling or disconnected hardware.


- **Immutability needs precise retention design.** A retention period that is too short weakens protection, while one that is too long may increase costs and introduce privacy concerns.


- **Multicloud backup needs an independent control plane.** Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce, Azure, and other clouds should not depend on one identity boundary, storage environment, or recovery path.


- **AI increases the speed and scale of change.** Copilots and AI agents can modify content, permissions, configurations, and workflows faster than manual recovery processes can track.


- **Recovery testing transforms protected copies into actionable evidence.** Teams should validate clean restore points, workload coverage, dependency order, and recovery time before an incident.


## **Systemic Risk: Why Backup Security Is Now a Board-Level Priority**


Ransomware is no longer the only force that can threaten your organization’s data. Sanctions, natural disasters, supply chain attacks, and regulatory shifts can each disrupt operations beyond your control. Analysts call this systemic risk — disruption at scale that no single organization can prevent. AI adds yet another element to the threat landscape. Even among enterprises confident in their defenses, 62% experienced AI-related unauthorized access in 2025. Confidence alone does not equate to protection. Backup security, data sovereignty, and immutable storage have become board-level priorities that help determine whether your business cancontinue operating during widespread disruption.


Encryption, isolation, air gaps, and immutability define whether your final line of defense holds when other controls fail. By themselves, they are also only claims. How a provider ensures immutability, handles encryption, and gives an organization to meet compliance, regulatory, and performance SLAs are often the difference between having a reliable backup copy and being stranded. Having a protected copy is still only half the equation. True resilience is measured by how quickly the business can operate again.


This post explains how


[AvePoint Cloud Backup](https://www.avepoint.com/products/cloud-backup) secures data by design, how sovereignty amplifies control, how air gaps and immutability work together, how to balance privacy with retention, and how the AvePoint Rapid Recovery System translates secure backups into rapid, prioritized recovery


.


## **Why Is Cloud Backup No Longer Optional?**


Moving to the cloud did not remove your responsibility for safeguarding your enterprise data. Microsoft, Google, Atlassian, Salesforce, and other vendors secure their infrastructure and keep their platforms available, while customers remain accountable for backup, access control, compliance, and recovery. A vendor cannot always tell between an intentional and unintentional deletion, a proper or improperly written script, a problematic migration, or an authorized and unauthorized configuration change.


That gap carries board-level weight: When backup fails, the business absorbs the downtime, compliance penalties, and reputational fallout, not the vendor. An unrecoverable system can disrupt revenue-generating operations, turning a technical oversight into a material business risk. That is why backup belongs on the board's risk agenda, not just on IT's shared-responsibility checklist.


Many organizations still confuse replication with backup. Geo-redundant replication keeps services running, but it copies deletions, corruption, and encrypted files just as faithfully as healthy data. Native recycle bins are time-limited and can be emptied by an attacker. Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, and Entra ID each need their own backup and recovery plan, yet Teams and Entra ID are often overlooked entirely.


## **How Does Cloud Backup Secure Data by Design?**


Backups are only as trustworthy as the controls around them.


[AvePoint Cloud Backup](https://www.avepoint.com/products/cloud-backup) applies security at every stage, from source to storage.


### Encryption in Transit and at Rest


Data in transit is always encrypted over TLS 1.2/1.3, and Cloud Backup uses only officially supported APIs that enforce encrypted connections. At rest, each customer tenant is protected by a unique AvePoint-managed key. Organizations that need more control can bring their own key (BYOK).


### Isolation and Least-Privilege Access


Backup data is segregated from your production environment and held outside the Microsoft trust boundary according to your policies. You can keep data in a single region, use multigeography configurations, or bring your own storage on Azure, AWS, or Google Cloud, and data is never replicated across data center regions. AvePoint operates data centers across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific, with recent additions in Singapore and South Africa to support regional compliance needs. Role-based access control lets you separate backup, restore, export, and administrative duties, so no single compromised account can undo your protection.


### Simple to Run, Independently Audited


[AvePoint Cloud Backup](https://www.avepoint.com/products/cloud-backup) requires no hardware, storage provisioning, or complex scripting, which leaves fewer moving parts to secure. AvePoint’s controls are independently audited against


[SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001:2022](https://www.avepoint.com/company/trust-center/compliance-certifications) ,


and US public sector and defense-industrial-base customers can use services that meet


[FedRAMP and CMMC Level 2](https://www.avepoint.com/company/trust-center/compliance-certifications) standards. These audits assess AvePoint's documentedlogical and physical access controls through least-privilege access policies.


## **Data Sovereignty: Why Is Control the New Currency of Trust?**


For business leaders, a lack of control is a strategic risk, not just a technical one.


[AvePoint Cloud Backup](https://www.avepoint.com/products/cloud-backup) maintains a separate, protected copy of your data outside your production environment, helping prevent a compromised tenant from affecting the same recovery path. This same need for control – over where your data lives, who can access it, and how backup copies are managed – is central to data sovereignty discussions that are quickly rising to the top of board agendas.


Ask ten organizations what data sovereignty means, and you'll get ten different answers because sovereignty isn't just about where a server sits. It's about layers of control: how much say you have over who can access your data, where it physically lives, and who can compel a vendor to provide access.


The question of sovereignty is urgent for two reasons:


- First, systemic risks – sanctions, regional conflicts, or outages – can isolate an organization from its cloud tenant entirely. In those moments, the ability to recover and continue operations matters most. Out of place recovery to standby tenants, cross subscription restoration, and even migration or repatriation from the cloud can provide additional resilience in these scenarios.


- Second, organizations are evaluating how vendors would respond if their home governments demand access to customer data. European leaders, in particular, are asking how American providers would protect their interests if that scenario arose,


[or if their staff will be sanctioned tomorrow](https://apnews.com/article/us-icc-trump-rubio-4ea3555403e3c695d8f81dc473515d9b) and cut off from accessing American technology.


There's no single right answer, because every organization and every regulator draws the line somewhere different. AvePoint gives you the flexible options to balance sovereignty, redundancy, isolation, security, and cost:


- **Bring Your Own Key (BYOK):** You hold the encryption key, so the service provider cannot read your data without access to the key only you control.


- **Bring Your Own Storage (BYOS):** Backup data copies are stored in storage owned and managed by the customer.


- **Regional data residency and Multi-Geo Support:** Your backup copies stay physically within the chosen country or region, never replicated elsewhere. For organizations with additional multigeography configurations in Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, AvePoint provides full support automatically routing data to the correct data center.


- **Sovereign and government clouds:** Environments like the UK Government Cloud meet in-country operational requirements — the same principle behind FedRAMP in the United States, IRAP in Australia, and similar frameworks worldwide. They're all the same demand for control, expressed differently.


- **Citizen-operated infrastructure:** Some organizations require that the people operating their environment are citizens of that country.


- **Data Replicas:** Additional Geo-Redundant data copies.


- **Deploy on Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud Platform:** Don’t just store independent backup copies but manage, process, and index your backups on a wholly independent cloud from your production system.


- **Repatriation:** The most extreme option is leaving the public cloud altogether and running infrastructure independently, with AvePoint supporting that transition where it's required.


Each layer adds control but can also increase costs. Greater forms of control, such as government clouds or repatriation, may also limit access to emerging capabilities such as AI or new integrations. Most organizations therefore select the tier that matches their real regulatory exposure rather than the most restrictive option available.


Flexibility is the defining feature of effective sovereignty. When requirements evolve – through legislation, court rulings, or shifting risk tolerance – your backup posture should adapt without unnecessary disruption. That adaptability, together with appropriate assurance and certification, supports a sovereignty strategy.

## How Should You Combine Air-Gapped and Immutable Backups?


Air gaps and immutability address different aspects of protection. An air-gapped backup is isolated from the production environment, limiting the paths by which attackers can reach it. An immutable backup prevents any modification or deletion for a set retention period, even if access is compromised. Combined, they preserve clean, recoverable data when it’s needed most.


For SaaS data, a physical air gap, such as tape in an offsite vault, is rarely practical.


[AvePoint Cloud Backup](https://www.avepoint.com/products/cloud-backup) instead delivers a logical air gap: Backup copies are segregated from your production tenant and separate access controls, so compromising production systems does not automatically give attackers access to your backups.


For immutability, AvePoint Cloud Backup supports two levels. Policy-based immutability prevents unauthorized users from deleting or modifying backup data for a set retention period. Authorized administrators can process a valid deletion request once that period ends or when applicable legal requirements permit the action. For organizations that require storage-level immutability, WORM (write once, read many) storage locks data the moment it's written — administrators and automated processes cannot alter or delete the protected data before the retention period expires. AvePoint also lets you set retention at the individual mailbox or user level rather than applying one policy across an entire backup set. For example, finance can keep seven years of records while Marketing keeps two, without either compromising the other.


A helpful benchmark is the


[3-2-1-1 rule](https://www.avepoint.com/blog/backup/what-is-the-3-2-1-backup-rule) — three copies of data, on two media types, with one offsite and one immutable or air-gapped. Properly configured immutability prevents deletion during the configured lock period, but short lock windows and misconfigured credentials can still create risk. Whatever the mix, test restores at least monthly. An immutable copy you cannot restore offers no protection.


## How Should You Balance Immutability with the Right to Be Forgotten?


Privacy laws can pull organizations in opposite directions. The GDPR expects the restoration of data availability after an incident, while Article 17 protects the right to erasure — mirrored by laws such as


South Africa's Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA). Meanwhile, frameworks like


HIPAA and the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) demand tamper-proof retention. The challenge lies in meeting both durability and deletion obligations without conflict.


Regulations such as HIPAA and PCI DSS also support tamper-proof data retention, which makes the balance harder to strike. A backup that can never change can also become a backup that cannot comply


With


[AvePoint Cloud Backup](https://www.avepoint.com/products/cloud-backup) , retention aligns with business and compliance mandates, keeping data only as long as required. Many backup vendors apply retention policies at the storage device, backup policy, connector level, or global level. AvePoint provides organizations with the ability to set retention down to the individual workload or container such as a mailbox, shared workspace, or personal drive.


Further, in the event of a verified erasure request (such as a Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) is received, administrators can approve deletion of the relevant data, ensuring privacy obligations are met without weakening protection.


That approval sits with authorized administrators only, and every action is logged: who requested the deletion, who approved it, and when it was carried out, giving you a defensible audit trail if a regulator ever asks. The same principle extends beyond backup to archived data, so a valid erasure request can't be satisfied in production while quietly surviving in a backup or archive copy.


For CDOs, CISOs and other leaders the takeaway is simple: choose controls that protect data integrity without locking you out of your privacy obligations.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **Are snapshots the same as immutable backups?**


Snapshots are not automatically immutable backups. A snapshot records a point in time, but administrators or attackers may still delete it unless storage-level controls prevent changes. Verify the lock mechanism, retention enforcement, identity boundary, and recovery workflow before treating a snapshot as a protected recovery point.


### **What is the difference between replication and an independent backup?**


Replication keeps another copy synchronized, while an independent backup preserves historical recovery points under separate controls. Replication can copy deletions, corruption, encryption, and bad configuration quickly. A backup should let teams select an earlier clean state and restore without depending on the source environment.


### **What is a good immutable retention target for most organizations?**


A good immutable retention target is the shortest period that meets recovery, legal, and audit needs with an acceptable cost. There is no universal number. Set targets by workload, then model normal deletion, ransomware dwell time, legal holds, and data subject obligations before approving the lock period.


### **Does Microsoft 365 Backup replace an independent backup copy?**


Microsoft 365 Backup provides a high-speed recovery layer for supported Microsoft 365 workloads, but it does not remove every need for an independent copy. Organizations may still require broader workload coverage, longer retention, granular restore, cross-tenant recovery, search, export, or storage outside the Microsoft trust boundary. Use each layer for its designed recovery scenario.


### **How does ransomware test an immutable backup strategy?**


Ransomware tests whether attackers can change retention, steal backup credentials, delete reachable copies, or force recovery from corrupted data. Immutability blocks alteration during the lock period, but only if the setting and identity path remain protected. Clean-point analysis and restore testing confirm that the locked copy is usable.


### **How often should backup policies and restore tests be reviewed?**


Backup policies and restore tests should be reviewed whenever workloads, regulations, recovery objectives, or business dependencies change. Critical services need more frequent testing than low-change archives. Many teams start with monthly tests for essential operations, quarterly tests for important workloads, and an annual cross-functional recovery exercise, then adjust using evidence.


### **What is WORM storage and how does it relate to immutability?**


Write once, read many storage prevents recorded data from being altered during a defined period. WORM is one technical method for delivering immutability. Teams still need encryption, access control, retention governance, search, and tested restore processes around the storage layer.


### **Do recycle bins and native retention count as backup?**


Recycle bins and native retention are recovery features, not complete independent backup strategies. They usually operate inside the same platform and administrative boundary as production data. Confirm time limits, workload coverage, administrator controls, search, export, and restore fidelity before relying on them for business recovery.


### **How do legal holds affect immutable backup retention?**


Legal holds suspend normal disposal for in-scope data until an authorized release. A backup design should identify held content, preserve evidence, and stop automatic expiration without extending unrelated data. Legal teams should define the scope and release conditions, while backup administrators implement and document each policy change.


### **What should security leaders ask a backup provider about AI-driven changes?**


Security leaders should ask whether the service can identify unusual change, preserve pre-change history, recover permissions and configuration, and show which automated identity caused an action. They should also ask whether AI agent definitions or workflows need separate protection. The answer should connect detection evidence to a tested recovery path.
